# Grinding Noise After Installing New Brakes: A Diagnostic Approach

A grinding noise upon braking immediately after swapping rotors and pads is a critical symptom that demands immediate attention, as it indicates metal-on-metal contact or severe component failure. In your specific scenario—where the driver's side functions correctly but the passenger side grinds despite new hardware—the issue likely stems from residual contamination or hydraulic pressure issues rather than misalignment of the new parts themselves.

The fact that you had to open the master reservoir cap and use the bleeding valve to retract the pistons is a significant red flag. This procedure suggests that the caliper was seized due to corrosion, not simply stuck from age. When a piston is forced out against high resistance without a proper hydraulic flush or pressure bleeder, it can introduce air into the system or fail to fully reseat. More critically, if the old pad material adhered to the rotor surface before removal, it may have been scraped off unevenly, leaving behind "hot spots" of hardened steel on the disc that will grind against fresh pads.

One potential source is a cross-contamination issue during installation. If you did not thoroughly clean the mating surfaces between the caliper bracket and the mounting bolts, or if there was old grease mixed with brake dust inside the caliper slide pins, the piston may have been partially blocked upon retraction. This creates an uneven pressure distribution across the pad. When one side of the rotor isn't fully clamped by the pads due to internal drag, the unclamped portion can skid against the metal backing plate or the rotor surface itself, generating that grinding sound.

Another possibility involves the rotor's condition post-removal. If the corroded caliper had been seized for a long time, it may have scored the rotor unevenly. Even with new pads, if the rotor was not machined (turned) to remove the deep grooves or rust pits created by the stuck piston, the new friction material might be riding over these imperfections rather than making full contact. This results in intermittent grinding as the pad contacts the high spots on the disc.

To diagnose this, you should lift the vehicle and spin the passenger-side rotor with your hand while applying light brake pressure to the pedal. If the noise persists without wheel rotation but stops when the wheels are free-spinning, the issue is likely internal caliper drag rather than a rotor surface defect. You can also perform a "spin test" on the installed pads; if they vibrate or shimmy slightly before locking up, it points to uneven pad torque or a stuck slider.

If the pistons do not retract smoothly after a second attempt with clean brake fluid and no air in the lines, the caliper may be internally corroded beyond repair. In this case, replacing the entire assembly is often safer than attempting to rebuild a seized unit, as internal corrosion can compromise structural integrity under heat stress.

While online forums occasionally suggest checking for misalignment of the new discs, rotors are generally pressed onto hubs with tight tolerances that prevent significant lateral movement unless the hub itself is damaged. The grinding is almost certainly hydraulic or surface-related. If the problem persists after bleeding and cleaning, inspecting the rotor runout with a dial indicator becomes necessary to rule out warped discs causing pulsation that mimics grinding.
